units.title: Typed interfaces, runtime validation and configuration
outcomes: Compare nominal and structural typing, generics with bounded TypeVars and variance, and justify where dynamic values are quarantined at the boundary.
Define a typed public API with protocols and generics that keeps persistence and transport types out of domain logic.
Build validated input models and typed settings with explicit unknown-field and precedence behavior, and diagnose one silent-corruption path.
units.why: Every later service in this section stands on this boundary. Untyped inputs and untyped configuration turn typos into silent corruption. Typed contracts with explicit validation move those failures to the edge where they are loud.

next.note: Carry the validated record into bounded JSONL and CSV ingestion with quarantine.
Expose the same typed service through the CLI surface.

focus: Protocol defines a static duck-typing boundary. Nominal inheritance is checked by name, structural compatibility by shape. Use Protocol for dependencies the domain calls but does not own.
Validate at the trust boundary with model_validate and model_validate_json. model_construct skips validation and is only for already-trusted data.
The default extra behavior ignores unknown fields, which silently drops data. Boundary models that must reject drift use extra forbid, and strict mode rejects coercions such as '3' to 3.

Settings precedence is init kwargs, then environment, then dotenv, then defaults. Unknown environment names are ignored, so a misspelled variable silently keeps the default, but an undefined key in the dotenv file raises under the default extra forbid.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, define a Protocol plus a generic service, a boundary model with extra forbid and a StrictInt field, and settings with a prefix. Show that model_validate coerces '3' in lax mode but strict rejects it with int_type, that an extra field raises extra_forbidden, and that init beats env beats default.
traps: runtime_checkable isinstance checks method presence only, not signatures. A sender with the wrong signature passes isinstance and fails later; keep static checking as the real gate.

parse_obj, .dict, .json and @validator still run, so old tutorials look current. In Pydantic 2.14 they are deprecated shims whose DeprecationWarning stays hidden outside __main__, and some v1 calls now fail: .json(indent=2) raises TypeError. Use model_validate, model_dump, model_dump_json and field_validator.

Expecting extra forbid to catch a misspelled environment variable. Unmatched environment names never reach validation (only undefined dotenv keys raise), so test precedence with a wrong-name variable and watch the default survive.

selfTest.q: A field x: int receives '123' in lax mode and under strict True. What happens in each?
selfTest.a: Lax coerces to 123. Strict raises with type int_type. Verified on Pydantic 2.14 with CPython 3.14.

selfTest.q: A payload carries an extra key y. How do default and extra forbid models differ?
selfTest.a: Default ignores y and dumps without it. Forbid raises extra_forbidden at ('y',).

selfTest.q: What are the v2 replacements for parse_obj and .dict, and why do the old names matter?
selfTest.a: model_validate and model_dump. The old names still run as deprecated shims that forward to the v2 methods, so legacy code looks current until v3 removes them, and some v1 signatures already fail: .json(indent=2) raises TypeError. Verified on Pydantic 2.14.1.

selfTest.q: Init passes port 9000, env sets 8080, default is 8000. Which wins, and what if the env name is misspelled?
selfTest.a: Init wins with 9000. A misspelled name is ignored and the default 8000 applies. Verified with pydantic-settings on CPython 3.14.

units.why: Ingestion is where outside bytes become inside facts. Unbounded reads, lenient parsing and lossy conversions turn one bad row into silent data loss. Explicit formats with quarantine keep the bad row visible and the good rows intact.

study.locator: Reading and Writing Single Files (write_table, read_table, the columns argument for subset reads); Finer-grained Reading and Writing (ParquetFile); Inspecting the Parquet File Metadata; Data Type Handling

focus: Row formats (JSON, JSONL, CSV) stream one record at a time. Parquet is columnar: a column-subset read skips the rest of the file.

Open CSV files with newline set to the empty string and let the csv module own line endings. Otherwise newline translation rewrites line breaks inside quoted fields, and Windows writes gain blank rows.
Parse one JSONL line at a time and quarantine JSONDecodeError with its line number, or one truncated line kills the whole file.

NaN and Infinity are Python extensions, not valid JSON. In Arrow, NaN is a float value and None is null: a table built with from_pylist or from_pydict keeps both through Parquet, while pandas folds them together (from_pandas writes NaN as null, to_pandas reads null as NaN).
units.reproduce: Closed-book, stream a mixed input with good rows, a truncated JSON line, and a quoted CSV field holding a comma and a newline, into quarantined normalized output in bounded memory. Convert it to Parquet with Table.from_pylist and assert schema types, None nulls preserved, NaN distinct from null, and a column-subset read.
traps: Splitting CSV on commas. Quoted commas, doubled quotes and embedded newlines need the csv module; the cookbook states this as a rule.

Round-tripping through pandas. from_pandas writes NaN as null and to_pandas reads null back as NaN, so a missing value and a failed computation become the same thing. Build the Arrow table with from_pylist or from_pydict and assert null_count.
list(reader) or json.load on a large file. Materializing the whole input removes the memory bound; iterate and write incrementally.

selfTest.q: What does json.loads('NaN') return, and is it valid JSON?
selfTest.a: Python returns nan, but NaN is not valid JSON. Guard reads with parse_constant and write with allow_nan False. Verified on CPython 3.14.

selfTest.q: Why open CSV files with newline set to the empty string?
selfTest.a: The csv module does its own line-ending handling. Without it, a quoted field holding \r\n reads back as \n, and on Windows every written row gains an extra \r that shows up as blank rows. Verified on CPython 3.14.

selfTest.q: How do you bound memory on a large JSONL file with bad lines?
selfTest.a: Iterate lines, parse one record at a time, and quarantine each JSONDecodeError with its line number. Never load the whole file.

selfTest.q: After a Parquet round trip, what happens to None and NaN?
selfTest.a: With a table built by from_pylist, None stays null and NaN stays NaN (null_count 1), and a columns subset read works. Through pandas they merge: from_pandas writes NaN as null, and to_pandas reads null as NaN. Verified with pyarrow 26 and pandas 3.0 on CPython 3.14.

units.title: Schema versions, compatibility and migrations
outcomes: Derive the valid states of a versioned record across validation, quarantine, normalization and persistence.
Design a backward-compatible schema change with explicit mixed-version behavior and a tested rollback.
Classify DDL changes as compatible or breaking, and run a paired upgrade and downgrade on a scratch database.
units.why: Schemas change while old readers are still running. An additive field with a default keeps both directions working, while a rename without a transition breaks one side silently. Version policy plus a tested downgrade makes evolution boring.

next.note: Apply constraints and normalization to the versioned schema.
Keep version checks at the service edge, not in handlers.

study.title: Creating and Modifying Tables
study.locator: Constraints in DDL (primary and foreign keys, UNIQUE, CHECK, DEFAULT); ALTER TABLE (adding and dropping columns, changing types, adding constraints); DROP TABLE, TRUNCATE and DELETE

focus: Additive changes (a new optional field, a new table) keep old readers working. Renames, type narrows and new required fields break one direction until every reader upgrades.
Every migration ships upgrade and downgrade together, and downgrade is executed, not just written. An empty downgrade makes rollback untested.
Alembic orders by down_revision chains, not file names. history --verbose shows the chain and current shows where the database stands.
Old payloads must validate against new models with defaults filling new fields, and new payloads must not crash old readers; the extra policy decides whether unknowns drop, stay or raise.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, evolve a v1 record model to v2 with one optional field: validate a v1 payload against v2 and a v2 payload against v1, stating what fills and what drops. Then write one Alembic revision with upgrade and downgrade and run upgrade head, downgrade base, upgrade head on a scratch database.
traps: extra forbid on a versioned reader. It rejects payloads from newer writers on unknown fields; versioned boundaries usually ignore or allow and stage the unknowns.
A new required field with existing rows. Old writers cannot supply it, and bulk backfill needs a default or a two-step migration.
Renaming a column while mixed versions read it. Old readers query the old name, so expand (add new, dual-write, migrate readers) before contracting (drop old).

selfTest.q: A v2 model adds nickname with a default. Does a v1 payload validate, and does a v1 model accept a v2 payload under default settings?
selfTest.a: Yes to both: the default fills nickname, and default extra ignore drops it on the old reader. Verified on Pydantic 2.14.

selfTest.q: What orders two Alembic revisions, and how do you inspect the chain?
selfTest.a: down_revision links order them, not filenames. history --verbose shows parents and current shows the database position.

selfTest.q: Name one DDL change that is safe under mixed versions and one that must wait.
selfTest.a: Adding a nullable column is safe. Renaming or dropping a column in use must wait until all readers upgrade.

selfTest.q: Why run downgrade base and then upgrade head when testing?
selfTest.a: It executes the rollback path and proves re-upgrade reaches the same schema. An unwritten or unrun downgrade is an untested promise.

units.title: Relational modeling, joins, aggregation and window functions
outcomes: Design a normalized schema with primary, foreign, unique and check constraints, and state which anomaly each normalization move fixes.
Predict row counts and duplicate behavior of multi-join queries before executing, including LEFT JOIN with WHERE and junction fan-out.
Write aggregation with HAVING, CTEs and window functions, and distinguish window row identity from GROUP BY collapsing.
units.why: ML features and labels come from joins and aggregations. A misplaced WHERE turns an outer join inner, and a GROUP BY at the wrong grain duplicates or drops rows. Predicting counts before running is the skill that prevents silent training-data corruption.

next.note: Guard the new schema with transactions and a retry policy.
Diagnose the slow joins with plans and selectivity.

study.locator: Deduplication with ROW_NUMBER; Top-\(N\) Per Group; ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK

focus: NULL never equals anything, not even NULL. Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL; COUNT(column) skips nulls while COUNT(*) does not.
ON filters before the outer join adds its nulls, WHERE filters after. A WHERE condition on the right table silently converts LEFT JOIN to INNER JOIN.
GROUP BY grain decides counts: aggregate at the wrong grain and rows duplicate or vanish. HAVING filters groups after aggregation, WHERE filters rows before.
Window functions keep row identity while GROUP BY collapses rows. ROW_NUMBER with PARTITION BY gives top-\(N\) per group without losing the row.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, on artists, tracks and streams tables: return every track with its stream count including zeros, per-artist totals with HAVING, and the top track per artist with ROW_NUMBER. Predict each row count before running.
traps: Selecting non-grouped columns under GROUP BY. PostgreSQL rejects them (SQLSTATE 42803) unless the table's primary key is grouped, while SQLite and relaxed-mode MySQL return a value from some row of the group; list exactly the grain.
A surrogate primary key preventing logical duplicates. It does not; only a UNIQUE constraint on the natural key does.
COUNT(*) when you mean COUNT(column). The first counts null-extended outer-join rows, the second skips the nulls.

selfTest.q: Tracks LEFT JOIN streams with WHERE streams.played_at > X. Which tracks survive?
selfTest.a: Only streamed tracks matching the filter: the WHERE removes null-extended rows and the join behaves inner. Move the filter to ON to keep all tracks.

selfTest.q: 5 artists and 12 tracks, each track with one artist. How many rows does the inner join return, and what changes with a junction table?
selfTest.a: 12 rows: each track matches exactly one artist. A many-to-many junction fans out: one track on two playlists yields two rows. Verified on PostgreSQL 18.6 with these sizes.

selfTest.q: When do you use HAVING instead of WHERE?
selfTest.a: To filter on aggregates after grouping, for example COUNT(*) > 2. WHERE cannot see aggregates.

selfTest.q: How does ROW_NUMBER top-1 per group differ from GROUP BY with max?
selfTest.a: ROW_NUMBER keeps the whole row including title and other columns. GROUP BY with max returns only the grouped columns plus the maximum.

units.title: Transactions, isolation anomalies and ORM boundaries
outcomes: Explain commit, rollback, savepoints and the PostgreSQL isolation anomaly table, including where PostgreSQL exceeds the standard.
Demonstrate one isolation anomaly or prevented anomaly on the live database at a named isolation level with the interleaving written out.
Draw the ORM transaction boundary with Session, identity map and eager loading, and fix one \(N+1\) with selectinload.
units.why: Concurrent writers share your tables. Without explicit transactions and a chosen isolation level, a retry or a second writer turns an invariant into a suggestion. The database prevents what you ask it to prevent, and nothing more.

next.note: Measure the plans behind the invariant checks.
Retried requests need transaction boundaries that make replay safe.

study.locator: Lazy Loading and Preventing unwanted lazy loads using raiseload; Joined Eager Loading; Select IN loading; What Kind of Loading to Use?

focus: PostgreSQL has three real levels: READ UNCOMMITTED behaves as READ COMMITTED, and REPEATABLE READ blocks phantom reads, which is stronger than the standard requires.

REPEATABLE READ takes its snapshot at the first non-transaction-control statement. An UPDATE of a row that another transaction changed and committed since then raises could not serialize access (SQLSTATE 40001), and the application retries the whole transaction.
The Session is the ORM transaction boundary plus an identity map: one object per primary key. Touching lazy relationships after commit issues new SELECTs or fails outside a session.
SAVEPOINT discards part of a transaction while keeping the rest. Forgetting COMMIT leaves an idle transaction that holds locks and bloats the database.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, run the two-session interleaving on PostgreSQL 18: session A begins REPEATABLE READ and reads balance 100; session B updates to 200 and commits; session A re-reads (still 100), commits, and reads 200. State the isolation level, the anomaly prevented, and the retry rule.
traps: REPEATABLE READ equals serializable. It does not: serialization anomalies are still possible, and only SERIALIZABLE plus retry logic on SQLSTATE 40001 prevents them.
No retry loop on serialization failures. Concurrent writers make these routine, not exceptional; abort and rerun the whole transaction.
Touching relationships after session close is free. Lazy loading fires one SELECT per parent (\(N+1\)) inside a session and fails outside it; use selectinload or joinedload and guard with raiseload.

selfTest.q: In the reproduce interleaving, what does session A read second, and why?
selfTest.a: 100. REPEATABLE READ holds the snapshot from the first statement of the transaction. After commit it reads 200. Verified on PostgreSQL 18.6.

selfTest.q: Which cells of Table 13.1 differ between the SQL standard and PostgreSQL?
selfTest.a: PostgreSQL READ UNCOMMITTED behaves as READ COMMITTED, and REPEATABLE READ has no phantom reads. Both guarantees are stronger than the standard minimums.

selfTest.q: A REPEATABLE READ update raises could not serialize access due to concurrent update. What does the application do?
selfTest.a: Roll back and retry the whole transaction from the beginning. The retried transaction sees the committed change in its new snapshot.

selfTest.q: Loading \(N\) parents then touching children issues how many statements under lazy loading, and after selectinload?
selfTest.a: \(N+1\) under lazy loading. With selectinload, one for the parents plus one IN query per 500 parent keys: 2 for 10 parents, 4 for 1200. Verified on SQLAlchemy 2.1.4.

study.title: PostgreSQL 14.1 Using EXPLAIN
study.locator: 14.1.1 EXPLAIN Basics: the sequential-scan cost as pages times seq_page_cost plus rows times cpu_tuple_cost, plus cpu_operator_cost per row for a WHERE check; 14.1.2 EXPLAIN ANALYZE; 14.1.3 Caveats

focus: High-selectivity equality predicates gain most. Low-selectivity filters and tiny tables stay on sequential scans, and every index taxes writes.
Equality columns come before range columns in composite indexes, and only the leftmost prefix is usable. A range column first wastes the rest.
EXPLAIN shows estimates and planner costs. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes and shows actual rows, loops, buffers and timing. Costs are planner units, not milliseconds.
Plans depend on statistics. State table size and ANALYZE state with every claim, and distrust toy-table plans.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, on a 5000-row ANALYZEd table of 32 pages with default cost settings: derive the sequential-scan cost for one equality filter from pages and rows before running EXPLAIN, add an index on the filter column, and compare EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) when the matching rows are scattered across the table and when they are clustered.
traps: Cost numbers are milliseconds. They are abstract planner units; only the EXPLAIN ANALYZE Execution Time is measured, on your hardware and cache state.
Wrapping an indexed column in a function. The predicate becomes unsargable and the plan falls back to a scan; rewrite the predicate or index the expression.
One index per column. Leftmost-prefix rules, OR conditions and implicit type conversions defeat single-column indexes; check the plan, not the schema.

selfTest.q: A 5000-row ANALYZEd table of 32 pages filters user_id = 7 with 100 matches. Where does the sequential scan's cost of 94.50 come from, and what does an index on user_id change?
selfTest.a: 32 pages times 1.0 plus 5000 rows times (0.01 + 0.0025) = 94.50. With the matches scattered over every page, the plan becomes a bitmap heap scan (cost 5.06 to 38.31) that still reads all 32 heap pages; with them clustered it is an index scan touching 4 buffers. Measured on PostgreSQL 18.6 with default costs.

selfTest.q: A filter has equality on status and a range on created_at. How do you order the composite index?
selfTest.a: Equality first, then range: (status, created_at). Range first wastes the second column under the leftmost rule.

selfTest.q: EXPLAIN estimates 10 rows but ANALYZE shows 4500 actual. What do you do first?
selfTest.a: Run ANALYZE and re-check. Stale or missing statistics is the first suspect before rewriting the query.

selfTest.q: Why can an index slow a workload down?
selfTest.a: Every write maintains each index, and unused or duplicate indexes cost storage and write amplification without speeding any read.

practice.name: Measured plan improvement on a scratch database
practice.locator: 14.1.2 EXPLAIN ANALYZE: before and after plans with BUFFERS for a selective filter plus a join from your service schema
practice.note: Use a scratch PostgreSQL 18 database (a throwaway postgres:18 container works) and a table over 1000 rows, run ANALYZE, and record pages, row counts, both plans, Heap Blocks and both execution times. Fix one anti-pattern from the lesson (function-wrapped column or SELECT star) and show the plan change.

units.stopWhen: You show before and after EXPLAIN ANALYZE with table size and ANALYZE state, explain why the selective case improved, and name one case on the same tables where the index does not help.

fit.note: The AlgoMaster index and EXPLAIN lessons plus the PostgreSQL Using EXPLAIN guide cover selectivity, plan reading and anti-patterns at measure depth, with the measurement done on the live database; no gap needed a new resource.

units.title: Layer boundaries and command-line contracts
outcomes: Split a service into domain, repository and notifier owners with dependency inversion, and swap fakes without touching the service.
Expose one service layer through a CLI with typed arguments, stdout data, stderr errors and nonzero exit on failure.
Keep transport and persistence types out of the domain core across both surfaces.
units.why: Providers change and transports multiply. When the domain depends on interfaces instead of concrete clients, a database or notifier swap stays local. When CLI and HTTP share one service layer, one fix covers both surfaces.

next.note: Expose the same service over HTTP with identical outcomes.

study.locator: The argparse built-in CLI parser block (positionals, flags, type, nargs, choices); Replaying the exact command line; then Subprocess and Shell Integration for returncode, stdout and stderr
study.depth: Skip the click, typer and fire pointers and the signal-handling block.

focus: The domain service takes repository and notifier interfaces in its constructor. Constructing concrete clients inside the service welds the boundary shut.
One sentence per class without and. A class that validates, prices, stores and notifies is four classes wearing one name.

argparse types and choices validate at the edge, and a bad argument already exits 2 with usage on stderr. Keep the same rule for domain failures: stdout carries data, stderr carries diagnostics, and failure exits nonzero with stdout left clean.
CLI and HTTP handlers call the same service function and map the same domain errors to the same outcomes.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, split an order processor into service, inventory and notifier with injected fakes, and drive it from a CLI: show a successful order on stdout with exit 0, and a bad choice plus missing input on stderr with nonzero exit.
traps: Business rules migrating into route handlers or CLI commands. Two surfaces then disagree; keep rules in the service and handlers thin.
Data mixed with logs on stdout. Pipes and files capture stdout, so diagnostics go to stderr or downstream parsing breaks.
Exit code always 0. A failed command that reports success poisons scripts and supervision; assert nonzero on every failure path.

selfTest.q: How do you swap the database for a fake without touching the service?
selfTest.a: The service depends on a repository interface and receives it by construction. The test constructs the service with the fake.

selfTest.q: Where do stdout and stderr go in a correct CLI, and what exits nonzero?
selfTest.a: Data on stdout, diagnostics on stderr. Every failure path exits nonzero with stdout clean.

selfTest.q: A route handler starts checking stock levels directly. What broke?
selfTest.a: The layer boundary: stock rules belong to the service and repository, and the handler should call the service and map its errors.

practice.note: Solve it from the Python starter, then reuse the split in your service: one test swaps both collaborators for fakes without editing OrderProcessor.

units.stopWhen: The service file imports no concrete adapter, the CLI drives success and two failure modes with correct streams and exits, and the fakes swap without service edits.

fit.note: The LLD interfaces and DIP lessons plus the one rehearsal problem cover dependency direction, FastAPI router layering covers transport separation, and the cookbook argparse block covers CLI parsing; no gap needed a new resource.

units.title: HTTP APIs, pagination, streaming and idempotency
outcomes: Expose the service over HTTP with request validation, response filtering, correct status codes and typed errors.
Ship capped limit-offset pagination and one streaming endpoint with bounded pages.
Implement idempotency keys so retried POSTs return the stored response with a single side effect, and mismatched replays error.
units.why: Retries are normal and duplicates are corruption. Validation plus status codes make failures legible, pagination bounds the response, and idempotency keys make a retried request safe to repeat.

next.note: Serve model-backed endpoints behind the same contract discipline.
Carry pagination and streaming into storage and network behavior.

study.title: Idempotent requests
study.locator: Idempotency-Key header with V4 UUID keys up to 255 characters; for API v1 the status code and body are saved once endpoint execution begins and replayed on retry, including 500s, while validation failures and concurrent conflicts save nothing; parameter-mismatch errors; keys on POST, never GET or DELETE; keys pruned after at least 24 hours

focus: One Pydantic model per request, one output model per response. Invalid bodies fail with 422 before any business logic runs.
The output model strips secrets: returning the input model leaks fields. Create returns 201, unknown ids return 404 with the detail envelope.

Defaults alone do not bound a page: a client can still send limit=1000000. Cap it with Query(le=...) so oversized requests fail with 422. Streams yield items under a declared AsyncIterable[Item] return type so validation and docs still apply.

The idempotency ledger stores, per key, the endpoint, a hash of the params and the saved response. A replay with the same hash returns the saved response; the same key with a different hash errors. Keys belong on POST: GET and DELETE are idempotent by definition.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, build a create endpoint with an output model, a capped paged list and an idempotency-key ledger: show 201 with secrets stripped, 422 on a bad body and on an oversized limit, 404 on an unknown id, a bounded page slice, and a double POST with one key producing one stored object.
traps: Returning the input model. Extra fields and secrets serialize to the client; a separate output model filters them, verified with TestClient on FastAPI 0.143.
Same idempotency key with new params silently accepted. Compare params and return a conflict, or a retry becomes an overwrite.

Check-then-insert on the ledger. Two concurrent first attempts both miss the lookup and both run the side effect; claim the key with a unique insert first, and answer a concurrent duplicate with a retryable conflict.

selfTest.q: A POST body misses a required field. What status, and when does business logic run?
selfTest.a: 422 from validation. Business logic never runs. Verified with TestClient on FastAPI 0.143.

selfTest.q: A client POSTs twice with the same key after a network timeout. How many objects exist and what does the second response carry?
selfTest.a: One object. The second response replays the saved status code and body. Stripe saves once endpoint execution begins, so a saved 500 replays too, while a request that failed validation saves nothing and can be retried.

selfTest.q: The same key arrives with different params. What happens?
selfTest.a: The server errors on the mismatch instead of applying the second params.

selfTest.q: GET /items would return 100000 rows. What breaks and what is the fix?
selfTest.a: Memory, latency and client parsing break. Page with skip and limit and cap limit with Query(le=...): a default alone does not stop limit=1000000. Or stream JSON Lines with a declared iterable type. Verified on FastAPI 0.143.
